title: From Blank Page to Written Argument
author: Stephany Anderson
summary: Stephany Anderson, a secondary English teacher, starts from the scene of ninth graders staring at a blank page on essay day even after outlining and analysing sample essays. She reframes the problem from why students will not write to how teachers help them find the words and get them onto the page. Her answer is writing to learn and talking to learn: low-stakes journaling before the assessment and structured peer conversation as a rehearsal space for academic language. She offers routines such as think-pair-share, text rendering and the 4 A's protocol, then two sustained models, the Science-Writing Heuristic and role-played dialogic argumentation with planning mnemonics such as STOP and DARE and TREE. Her conclusion is that outlines, organizers and rubrics cannot supply language students have never practiced using, so collaborative talk and writing prepare students for independent work rather than lowering expectations.
points: Writing is a way to develop learning as well as to demonstrate it, so students need regular low-stakes writing before any graded essay.
Oral language development strengthens writing because students often need to hear, try and revise disciplinary language before they can use it independently.
The Science-Writing Heuristic moves students from individual written meaning-making to group negotiation to comparison with authoritative sources, and adapts beyond science.
Role-playing both sides of an issue before drafting forces students to reach for different claims, evidence and vocabulary, which improves the argument they later write.
Outlines, graphic organizers and rubrics cannot supply vocabulary students have not practiced, so rehearsal through talk is what shortens the pause on essay day.
quotes: But writing is not only a way to demonstrate learning. It is also a way to develop learning.

A few minutes of low-stakes writing each day helps students collect ideas, rehearse language, and discover what they think. By essay day, they have a trail of words behind them, so are not beginning with nothing.
Structured peer conversation gives students a rehearsal space for writing. Then when they face the blank page, the words are not entirely new. They have already spoken some of them aloud.
Students must first put their own thinking into words and then use those words to build knowledge with others.
To speak from another perspective, students must reach for different claims, evidence, and vocabulary.

An outline can organize ideas, but it cannot supply language students have never practiced using. A graphic organizer can hold evidence, but it cannot replace the intellectual work of discussing what that evidence means.
Collaborative writing and structured talk do not lower expectations for independent work. They prepare students to meet those expectations.
